articles.title: Commercial Real Estate Industry Report

citations.text: English manuscript and evidence appendix · Evidence records · Value-chain graphic
notes: Industry report · Version 1.0 · Published: 30 October 2026 · Research cutoff: 28 October 2026.
Cover: AI-generated architectural illustration. It is not a photograph of One Vanderbilt or documentary evidence of the opening transaction.

The report covers income-producing offices, retail, logistics, hotels and data centers, with institutional rental housing included where source universes include it. The framework is global; company examples and financing analysis emphasize the United States, with Europe and mainland China as comparisons. Market size and sector shares refer to 2025; trading conditions cover H1 2026; the separate U.S. listed REIT snapshot is dated 30 September 2026. These are dated observations, not a claim of complete October market coverage.

Our assessment is that commercial real estate is recovering unevenly. A useful analysis connects tenant demand and the cost of keeping a building competitive with the owner’s debt schedule. Transaction recovery can improve liquidity while an individual property still requires new equity.

articles.title: Minor Metals Industry Report

citations.text: Cover: a real antimony metal specimen, photographed on 23 March 2009. Photo: Jurii / Wikimedia Commons · images-of-elements.com · CC BY 3.0 . Cropped and converted to WebP. View the full photograph .
notes: Industry report · Version 1.1 · Published: 28 October 2026 · Research cutoff: 27 October 2026.

This report examines global minor-metal supply chains, focusing on tungsten, antimony, gallium, germanium, indium, bismuth and molybdenum. Niobium, rhenium, tellurium and selenium provide adjacent-market examples. It does not comprehensively cover rare earths, lithium–nickel–cobalt battery materials or precious metals. Research closes on 27 October 2026. Production charts use the 2024 statistical period in the BGS publication released in 2026; company cases mainly cover disclosures for 2025–2026. The central assessment is that commercial value depends on converting feedstock consistently into customer-qualified material that can be delivered on time. Resources, processing capability, permission to trade and cash flow must be assessed together.

articles.title: Global Healthcare Industry Report

citations.text: English manuscript · Evidence records
notes: Industry report · Version 1.1 · Published: 27 October 2026 · Research cutoff: 26 October 2026.
Cover: AI-generated concept image of a hospital and IV bag. It does not depict Baxter, North Cove or the hurricane.

A global industry framework with quantitative case studies from the United States and China. This is an industry overview; its quantitative findings do not represent every region or healthcare submarket. The industry boundary includes medicines, medical devices and diagnostics, research and manufacturing services, distribution, clinical care and payment. Consumer wellness, beauty products and general fitness are excluded. Research cutoff is 26 October 2026. Data periods differ and are identified locally. The global spending figure is an explicitly historical 2022 baseline, not the latest GHED observation or a 2026 market estimate.

DEX assessment: durable commercial value is most likely where a business can demonstrate clinical usefulness, obtain a workable payment route and deliver reliably. More demand or a larger revenue base alone does not establish stronger profits. The analysis below separates observed facts from mechanisms and research hypotheses.

Supports: China had 3.287 million registered drones at year-end 2025, up 51.0%. Drones accumulated 45.3029 million flight hours in 2025, up 69.89%. The country had 46 low-altitude flight service stations across 23 provincial-level regions.

citations.section: [C02] Interim Regulations on the Flight Management of Unmanned Aircraft
citations.text: Read: 2026-10-19 | Original source
notes: State Council and Central Military Commission; official text on the Chinese government portal | Primary regulation text.
Published: 28 June 2023. | Event: Order No. 761 dated 31 May 2023; effective 1 January 2024.

Period / scope: Applicable framework at the research cutoff, read together with later aviation law and implementing rules; People's Republic of China; Separate layers for airworthiness, operator certification, liability insurance, pilot requirements, airspace and flight applications.
Location: Articles 8, 11, 12, 19, 26, 31 and 32; full regulation read.

Supports: Effective January 1, 2024. Articles 8, 11 and 12 separately address airworthiness, operator certification and liability insurance. Controlled airspace requires approval. Article 26 allows long-term applications for routine flights in fixed airspace. Article 31 retains application requirements for specified operations, including relayed flights and dropping items; Article 32 requires collision-avoidance measures for BVLOS flight.

Limits: An operator certificate is not blanket permission to use any route or airspace. Airspace below 120 metres is not universally unrestricted. This is a framework summary, not case-specific compliance advice.

citations.section: [C03] Civil Aviation Law of the People's Republic of China, effective July 1, 2026
citations.text: Read: 2026-10-19 | Original source
notes: Standing Committee of the National People's Congress; official text published by CAAC | Primary legislation.
Published: 27 December 2025. | Event: Revision adopted on 27 December 2025; effective 1 July 2026.

Period / scope: In force from 1 July 2026, before the research cutoff; China; Aviation-law requirements for unmanned aircraft airworthiness and product identification, retaining prescribed exemptions and special-rule provisions.
Location: Articles 34, 258 and 262; full law text read.

Supports: The December 27, 2025 revision took effect on July 1, 2026. Article 34 embeds unmanned aircraft airworthiness requirements in the aviation law, retaining exemptions prescribed by national rules, and requires manufacturers to assign a unique product identifier. Article 258 preserves special State Council and Central Military Commission rules for unmanned aircraft.
Limits: The law does not imply that every small drone needs a type certificate after July 2026. The exemptions and interaction with special drone rules must remain explicit.

Supports: Effective October 9, 2025 through December 31, 2026. Eligible small-drone new routes reaching 5,000 annual flights can receive RMB200,000 once. notes: Nisingizwe et al; The Lancet Global Health | Primary peer-reviewed observational study; publisher-format full text read through a UPDWG-hosted copy.

Published: April 2022 journal issue, volume 10, pages e564–e569; exact online-first date not shown in the examined PDF. | Event: Drone orders from 17 March 2017 to 31 December 2019; facility administrative data begin in January 2015.

Period / scope: 2015–2019 facility study; delivery comparison uses March 2017–December 2019 orders; expiry effect is assessed at 12 months after implementation; Twenty district and provincial health facilities in Rwanda; Blood-product orders, delivery minutes and expired blood units. The 49.6-minute overall mean includes preparation; the road comparison uses a 41-minute drone median excluding preparation and estimated road medians.
Location: Page e564, abstract; e566, methods and Table 1; e567, delivery-time results; e568, discussion and limitations. DOI: 10.1016/S2214-109X(22)00048-1.

Supports: The study covers 12,733 drone blood-product orders at 20 Rwandan facilities; 43% were emergencies. Overall mean drone delivery time was 49.6 minutes including preparation and packaging. citations.text: Read: 2026-10-19 | Original source

Supports: In a laboratory test, 38 normal-hearing community participants rated 103 sounds. citations.text: Read: 2026-10-19 | Original source

DEX RESEARCH
Passenger vehicles and the electric mobility value chain
18 October 2026 | English manuscript

Electric mobility has reached substantial scale, but growth, profit and dependable service are different achievements. This report follows a fast-charging launch through industry history, regional markets, the value chain and company economics. Its central assessment is that competitive strength depends on turning technology into repeatable manufacturing, affordable ownership and reliable energy access, with returns evaluated within each business and statistical boundary.

Global research with emphasis on China, Europe and North America. Passenger BEVs and PHEVs, including EREVs where included by the source, form the core. Commercial vehicles and fuel-cell vehicles are separate context. Public information available through 18 October 2026. The SNE group share chart explicitly covers a broader BEV plus PHEV market including commercial vehicles in 80 countries. Complete-year 2025 results and 2026 interim observations remain separate.
Contents Part 1 Industry Story · Part 2 Industry History · Part 3 Market Landscape · Part 4 Industry Challenges · Supporting Evidence

articles.title: Global Agricultural Technology and Equipment Industry Brief

citations.text: English manuscript · Supporting Evidence records
notes: Industry report · Version 1.0 · Global scope · Public information through 16 October 2026.
Planter and tractor at Frick Farms, northeast Texas, 13 April 2021. USDA photo by Lance Cheung. Public Domain Mark 1.0. [I01] View original photograph · 4096 × 2731

Agricultural technology and equipment convert power, location data, crop observations and agronomic decisions into work in the field. This report examines machinery, precision agriculture, agricultural drones and robots, irrigation and digital agriculture worldwide, with detailed comparisons of China, North America, Europe and India. Seeds, crop protection chemicals and biotechnology appear as related inputs; their entire industries are outside the core market boundary.

The evidence points to an industry whose commercial results depend on the farming system. Large equipment platforms, retrofits, specialist irrigation systems and contracted field services address different buyers. A technology can reduce an input on a particular field while still failing to earn its purchase and operating costs. This report therefore connects product capabilities with seasonal utilization, service access and farm economics, and treats company performance separately from claims about technology effectiveness.

The four Parts cover a documented industry story, history, the value chain and market landscape, and operating challenges. The company table preserves reporting periods, currencies and business scopes. The share chart covers only FADA's Indian tractor retail registration categories in FY2025-26. The independent Supporting Evidence appendix records what each source supports, its dates and limitations. Dates of publication, observation and financial reporting are kept distinct.

The ERS report documents digital-agriculture adoption from 1996 to 2019 using the Agricultural Resource Management Survey. articles.title: Global Nuclear Equipment and Services Industry Brief

citations.text: Full English manuscript Supporting Evidence Capacity data CSV
notes: Industry report · Version 1.0 · Global scope · Public information cutoff 13 October 2026.

Reactor hall at the existing Dukovany Nuclear Power Plant, Czech Republic, 6 November 2012. Photo: Petr Pavlicek / IAEA, IAEA Imagebank, CC BY-SA 2.0. Used unchanged as an industry illustration; it does not show the later Dukovany new-build project. [I01]

This report examines the global suppliers of equipment, engineering, fuel-cycle processing and technical services used by civilian nuclear-power plants. It covers construction, operation, life extension and the back end. Uranium feed appears as supply-chain context; electricity sales, uranium mining revenue, military uses and medical-isotope revenue are outside the market boundary.

The commercial opportunity depends on both new projects and the existing fleet. The report follows how qualified equipment becomes an operating plant and how long-term fuel, inspection and maintenance contracts create service demand. Announced projects, orders, revenue and cash flow represent different stages. The analysis uses original disclosures and preserves their reporting periods and business boundaries.

Sources were reviewed on 13 October 2026, with a public-information cutoff of that date. No unified global equipment-and-services revenue total is asserted. The share figure is explicitly limited to 2025 uranium-enrichment service capacity. Future production dates remain company plans. This is version 1.0.

2025 revenue was EUR 5,399 million, new orders EUR 5,924 million and EBITDA EUR 665 million; Growth involved EPR projects, fuel, I&C and installed-base services; Major-component work included North America and South Africa; replacement of four steam generators at Flamanville 2 began in November 2025. Limit: Use Framatome's own reporting perimeter; its footnote identifies EUR 641 million under EDF reporting, which must not be mixed with EUR 665 million; avoid the potentially stale ownership boilerplate.

2025 revenue was EUR 2,096.2 million and the year-end order book EUR 21.3 billion; Contracted orders extend into the 2040s. Limit: The order book spans multiple years rather than current revenue; exchange rates affect its euro value; it is not reactor-equipment revenue or global equipment market share.

2025 group revenue was EUR 5,138 million; A one-off Japanese-utility back-end contract contribution raised the 2024 comparison base; Revised end-of-lifecycle estimates affected 2025 adjusted earnings. Limit: The group includes mining and other activities; group revenue and its annual change do not measure the reactor-maintenance market.

Segments comprise Mining, Front End (Chemistry and Enrichment), and Back End (Recycling, Nuclear Packages and Services, Dismantling and Services, Engineering); Back End revenue was EUR 2,352 million in 2025. Limit: Back End includes recycling, packages and engineering and is not pure decommissioning revenue; publication date is not displayed.

Commercial Operations revenue was USD 853.070 million in 2025, with approximately USD 1,720 million in year-end backlog; The segment supplies heavy nuclear components, fuel, engineering and maintenance and also includes medical isotope and pharmaceutical-related activities; Kinectrics acquisition closed on May 20, 2025 and entered Commercial Operations; Commercial contracts include fixed-price and time-and-materials arrangements, with large custom-component and service revenue generally recognised over time. Limit: Commercial Operations is not pure civilian nuclear-power revenue; acquisitions affect growth; government and naval nuclear work is separate; backlog methodology need not match peers; date is the report signature date.

Commercial Operations revenue was USD 586.158 million in H1 2026; The segment's June 30 backlog was USD 1,600.454 million; Q2 growth included nuclear components, field services, fuel handling, medical activities and Kinectrics. Limit: Interim results are unaudited, include medical activities and acquisition effects, and should not be annualised by simple doubling.

2025 group sales were USD 3,498.372 million; Naval & Power sales were USD 1,503.002 million; Commercial nuclear solutions grew, while the segment also includes naval and process-industry activities. Limit: Neither figure is pure nuclear-power equipment-and-service revenue; total orders and backlog also include aerospace, defence and other business.

Supplies reactor-coolant-pump technology for AP1000; Provides nuclear products, parts, I&C, testing, field and obsolescence support, alongside defence nuclear business. Limit: Installed-product coverage and self-described leadership do not establish exclusive revenue market share; no publication date is shown.

A contract of about KRW 320 billion covers two steam-turbine and turbine-control-system sets for Dukovany 5 and 6; The counterparty is Czech subsidiary Doosan Skoda Power; ceremony held February 16, 2026; KHNP signed the principal project contract in June 2025. Limit: An intra-group contract cannot simply be added as sales of both companies; contract value is not current-year revenue or proof of commissioning.

Products include reactor and internals, steam generators, coolant pumps, pressurisers and fuel-handling equipment; MMIS covers control, monitoring, instrumentation and emergency safety functions. Limit: Do not use the company's unqualified 'largest supplier' claim as a ranking; equipment configurations differ by reactor type.

Supplies large castings and forgings for nuclear reactors and steam generators as well as turbine and generator components. Limit: The business also serves other generation technologies and industrial users; no pure nuclear revenue or share is established.

Provides component replacement, repair/refurbishment, routine and outage maintenance, upgrades, engineering and I&C replacement. Limit: A service menu identifies capabilities rather than revenue or a specific current contract for every offering.

The current name is GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy (GVH); Provides reactor technology, fuel and nuclear services; GE Vernova-led GNF operates fuel plants; Canadian activities support BWRX-300 deployment. Limit: GE Vernova group revenue must not be treated as nuclear-business revenue; the page has no publication date.

Activities span uranium production, enrichment, fabrication, domestic and international nuclear construction, generation and spent-fuel/radioactive-waste management. Limit: Self-reported rankings are not independent market-share evidence; generation and non-nuclear businesses broaden the group perimeter; total revenue is not an equipment-service market estimate; publication date is not stated.

Maintains turbines, generators and other turbine-island equipment and supports upgrades and life extension; Services legacy equipment from other manufacturers and offers multi-year agreements. Limit: Supplier support is not regulatory authority to grant life extension; customer or installed-base coverage is not exclusive share.

Has serial-supply capabilities for nuclear-island main equipment and turbine-generator sets for the conventional island. Limit: Group capabilities differ from listed-company financial scope; unqualified leadership/share language is not used; no publication date is shown.

H1 2026 revenue was EUR 2,696 million and EBITDA EUR 595 million; The company attributed Mining and Front End disruption to exceptional weather. Limit: Group results span multiple activities; do not extrapolate the half-year result; operational attribution is management's explanation.

EDF reports Framatome sales of EUR 5,372 million and Arabelle Solutions sales of EUR 990 million. Limit: Different from Framatome's own EUR 5,399 million disclosure; this source does not separately explain the EUR 27 million sales difference, so no specific cause is inferred; EDF electricity sales are not equipment-service revenue.

Manufactures reactor-pressure-vessel and steam-generator components and turbine/generator shafts; Highlights steelmaking, forging, heat treatment and large machining, and notes standardisation limits in build-to-order production. Limit: Used for manufacturing processes and business types rather than 2026 capacity; unqualified market-leadership claims are excluded.

The report lists Guohe-series reactor-coolant pumps and nuclear-island/conventional-island equipment supplied to Zhangzhou unit 1. Limit: Used as company evidence of equipment roles; total group revenue is not nuclear revenue, and no ranking without a comparable denominator is adopted.

KHNP signed the final two-unit Dukovany contract in June 2025; Its Barakah role includes joint project management and operating-support/long-term-maintenance agreements; Its El-Dabaa scope covers turbine-island construction for four VVER-1200 units. Limit: Contract scope differs by project; operator total revenue does not identify equipment/service revenue; no publication date is displayed.

Signed the Dukovany 5/6 A/E-services contract with KHNP on December 12, 2025; Scope includes auxiliary-equipment procurement and licensing support. Limit: This subcontracted engineering scope is neither total project investment nor fully recognised 2025 revenue.

Bechtel and Westinghouse selected Arabelle to supply three turbine-generator sets and related turbine-island equipment for Poland; Arabelle is an EDF Group subsidiary. Limit: Selection does not establish full financing, construction start or commercial operation; no contract value is stated; do not compare its ranking with nuclear-island suppliers.

Provides materials/component testing, safety and licensing support, outage inspections, lifecycle and waste management. Limit: The service catalogue is not revenue segmentation; parent-company relationship is evidenced by V07.

Safety-related parts require quality records, design compatibility and acceptance criteria; some OEMs reduce support or exit; Commercial-grade dedication, inspections and witnessed tests support qualification for nuclear use. Limit: Company guidance is not the governing regulation and does not imply unconditional acceptance of every commercial item in safety-related equipment.

Supports integrated plant assessment, time-limited aging analyses and environmental reporting; Licence extension requires regulatory approval. Limit: Supplier technical support does not replace regulatory approval; jurisdiction-specific rules require separate verification.

Long-term-operation services cover licence renewal, aging and asset management, modernisation and upgrades. Limit: The page describes capabilities rather than approval of a particular plant extension; publication date comes from structured page metadata.

WNA, Uranium Enrichment, updated 2026-09-29; 2025 global capacity; thousand SWU/year; capacity table and footnote. Supports enrichment-capacity composition; CNNC is estimated. Rows total 68,077 versus reported 68,076; author calculations use rows. The source does not explain the difference. Capacity is not revenue or deliveries.

WNA, World Nuclear Power Reactors & Uranium Requirements, updated 2026-10-08; global status snapshot; reactors/MWe; WORLD row and Notes. Supports fleet and construction indicators. Operable means grid-connected; construction includes suspended projects. Operable capacity is net and construction capacity gross; do not sum them.

Urenco, Full year 2025 audited financial results, published 2026-03-12; FY2025/2025-12-31 backlog; global group; EUR; Financial highlights/Outlook. Supports €2,096.2m revenue and €21.3bn backlog. Backlog spans multiple years; group scope and exchange-rate effects prevent treating it as annual segment-market size.

Urenco, Half year 2026 unaudited financial results, published 2026-08-13; H1 2026/2026-06-30; global group; EUR; Summary/backlog discussion. Supports €27.3bn backlog, €645.4m revenue and the delivery-timing explanation. Unaudited; do not mechanically annualize or infer falling demand from one revenue period.

Orano, Annual Activity Report 2025, issued 2026; exact PDF publication date not displayed; FY2025 and 2028–2030 expansion plans; French facility/global customers; million SWU/year; printed p.39. Supports 7.5 million existing capacity, 2.5 million expansion and its schedule. Expansion is prospective; the approximately 50-million-SWU demand market described in the report cannot replace the WNA capacity denominator.

Orano, 2026 Half-year Results, published 2026-07-31; H1/2026-06-30; global group; EUR; printed pp.2–3 and definitions. Supports €2,696m revenue, €34,393m backlog and €619m Front End revenue. Group figures include mining; Front End combines conversion and enrichment. Neither is a pure enrichment/equipment market total; backlog is a multi-year valuation.

EDF, Management Report 2025, released with results on 2026-02-20; FY2025; global Framatome/Arabelle; EUR; printed pp.10–11. EDF reports €5,372m Framatome sales versus €5,399m in M12. A complete revenue reconciliation is not provided in the reviewed texts. The narrative consistently uses M12.

EDF, 2026 half-year results, published 2026-07-31; H1 2026; global Framatome; EUR; printed p.6. Supports order intake of about €2.7bn and contributions from Installed Base/Fuel activities and EPR2 component production. Industry and services sales include other businesses and cannot be labelled Framatome sales; EBITDA, revenue and orders are distinct measures.

GE Vernova, 2025 Annual Report/10-K, issued 2026; FY2025; global; USD; 10-K printed pp.5 and 26. Supports Nuclear Power revenue of US$1,018m and BWR, fuel and SMR scope. Some nuclear-turbine activities sit in Steam Power, which also includes coal; total group/Power revenue is not nuclear revenue.

BWXT, FY2025 Form 10-K, signed 2026-02-23; FY2025; global group; USD; printed p.36, Commercial Operations. Supports US$853.070m revenue and US$231.0m acquisition contribution. Commercial Operations includes medical activities; group scope includes government/naval nuclear work. Growth is not entirely organic, and these figures cannot establish pure civil nuclear-power shares.

EDF, Universal Registration Document 2025, English PDF dated 2026-04-02; FY2025; global Framatome; product scope/reactors; printed pp.41–43. Supports nuclear steam-supply systems, instrumentation and control, fuel and operating-plant services, and work on more than 380 reactors. Service coverage overlaps and is not exclusive share; company scope also includes defence and healthcare.

Framatome, Framatome reports 2025 financial results, published 2026-03-04; FY2025; global group; EUR; financial table, commentary and EBITDA footnote. Supports €5,399m revenue, €5,924m orders and €665m EBITDA. The footnote explains adjustments versus EDF's €641m EBITDA; it does not separately reconcile the revenue difference. Adjacent businesses prevent treating group revenue as a pure nuclear-power market share.

Supports Bechtel's 2017 appointment and project staffing. Project figures and supplier assessments cannot establish global industry outcomes.

The 2017 brochure supports treaty dates and obligation scope. Historical party counts are not presented as current.
Supports the 2022 estimate and weld-process issue. EUR 13.2 billion uses 2015 prices, excluding construction-period interest; final costs are unproven.
Supports first grid connection and further testing in December 2024. It does not establish full-power or sustained performance.
Supports ageing assessments and auditable documentation. Technical guidance does not substitute for plant-specific regulatory permission.
Supports Browns Ferry's 2025 permissions and reviews. Plant-specific permission cannot establish 80-year operation for all reactors.
The 2023 article supports SMR definition, examples and economic uncertainty. Historic design counts are not current totals.
Supports six 2024 deconversion frameworks. Contract ceilings and eligibility establish neither material delivery nor realised revenue.
Supports Sizewell C's decision, financing and target. Costs in 2024 prices and projected benefits are not realised results.
The 2019 report informs ageing-fleet history. Its capacity and average-age figures are not treated as current.
Supports financing and enrichment concentration in 2025. Capacity, revenue and future scenarios measure different things.
Supports the October 2026 workforce programme. Graduate numbers, resolved shortages and productivity gains are not demonstrated.
Supports April 2026 construction progress and EPC role. Commercial operation, competitive cost and regulatory firsts are not established.

Supports Calder Hall's 1956 opening. The article's conflicting, unqualified first-grid claim is excluded.

Year-end conversion-service commitments totalled about 83 million kgU of UF6; Westinghouse participates as a subcontractor in the KHNP-led Dukovany project and has fuel-fabrication responsibilities for a specified period. Limit: Conversion kgU differs from enrichment SWU; the page does not state its publication date; Cameco's ownership-share figures are not Westinghouse's 100% revenue.

Westinghouse Operating Plants includes engineered equipment, reactor services and fuel products and services; Most recurring business is secured in advance under contracts lasting three to more than ten years; Cameco Fuel Services includes UO2, UF6 and heavy-water-reactor fuel bundles. Limit: Management's recurring-business description does not guarantee quarterly growth; customer coverage is not exclusive market share; illustrative economics in this section are not forecasts or guidance; publication date not independently verified.

2025 revenue was EUR 5,399 million, new orders EUR 5,924 million and EBITDA EUR 665 million; Growth involved EPR projects, fuel, I&C and installed-base services; Major-component work included North America and South Africa; replacement of four steam generators at Flamanville 2 began in November 2025. Limit: Use Framatome's own reporting perimeter; its footnote identifies EUR 641 million under EDF reporting, which must not be mixed with EUR 665 million; avoid the potentially stale ownership boilerplate.

2025 revenue was EUR 2,096.2 million and the year-end order book EUR 21.3 billion; Contracted orders extend into the 2040s. Limit: The order book spans multiple years rather than current revenue; exchange rates affect its euro value; it is not reactor-equipment revenue or global equipment market share.

2025 group revenue was EUR 5,138 million; A one-off Japanese-utility back-end contract contribution raised the 2024 comparison base; Revised end-of-lifecycle estimates affected 2025 adjusted earnings. Limit: The group includes mining and other activities; group revenue and its annual change do not measure the reactor-maintenance market.

Segments comprise Mining, Front End (Chemistry and Enrichment), and Back End (Recycling, Nuclear Packages and Services, Dismantling and Services, Engineering); Back End revenue was EUR 2,352 million in 2025. Limit: Back End includes recycling, packages and engineering and is not pure decommissioning revenue; publication date is not displayed.

Commercial Operations revenue was USD 853.070 million in 2025, with approximately USD 1,720 million in year-end backlog; The segment supplies heavy nuclear components, fuel, engineering and maintenance and also includes medical isotope and pharmaceutical-related activities; Kinectrics acquisition closed on May 20, 2025 and entered Commercial Operations; Commercial contracts include fixed-price and time-and-materials arrangements, with large custom-component and service revenue generally recognised over time. Limit: Commercial Operations is not pure civilian nuclear-power revenue; acquisitions affect growth; government and naval nuclear work is separate; backlog methodology need not match peers; date is the report signature date.

Commercial Operations revenue was USD 586.158 million in H1 2026; The segment's June 30 backlog was USD 1,600.454 million; Q2 growth included nuclear components, field services, fuel handling, medical activities and Kinectrics. Limit: Interim results are unaudited, include medical activities and acquisition effects, and should not be annualised by simple doubling.

2025 group sales were USD 3,498.372 million; Naval & Power sales were USD 1,503.002 million; Commercial nuclear solutions grew, while the segment also includes naval and process-industry activities. Limit: Neither figure is pure nuclear-power equipment-and-service revenue; total orders and backlog also include aerospace, defence and other business.

Supplies reactor-coolant-pump technology for AP1000; Provides nuclear products, parts, I&C, testing, field and obsolescence support, alongside defence nuclear business. Limit: Installed-product coverage and self-described leadership do not establish exclusive revenue market share; no publication date is shown.

A contract of about KRW 320 billion covers two steam-turbine and turbine-control-system sets for Dukovany 5 and 6; The counterparty is Czech subsidiary Doosan Skoda Power; ceremony held February 16, 2026; KHNP signed the principal project contract in June 2025. Limit: An intra-group contract cannot simply be added as sales of both companies; contract value is not current-year revenue or proof of commissioning.

Products include reactor and internals, steam generators, coolant pumps, pressurisers and fuel-handling equipment; MMIS covers control, monitoring, instrumentation and emergency safety functions. Limit: Do not use the company's unqualified 'largest supplier' claim as a ranking; equipment configurations differ by reactor type.

Supplies large castings and forgings for nuclear reactors and steam generators as well as turbine and generator components. Limit: The business also serves other generation technologies and industrial users; no pure nuclear revenue or share is established.

Provides component replacement, repair/refurbishment, routine and outage maintenance, upgrades, engineering and I&C replacement. Limit: A service menu identifies capabilities rather than revenue or a specific current contract for every offering.

The current name is GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy (GVH); Provides reactor technology, fuel and nuclear services; GE Vernova-led GNF operates fuel plants; Canadian activities support BWRX-300 deployment. Limit: GE Vernova group revenue must not be treated as nuclear-business revenue; the page has no publication date.

Activities span uranium production, enrichment, fabrication, domestic and international nuclear construction, generation and spent-fuel/radioactive-waste management. Limit: Self-reported rankings are not independent market-share evidence; generation and non-nuclear businesses broaden the group perimeter; total revenue is not an equipment-service market estimate; publication date is not stated.

Maintains turbines, generators and other turbine-island equipment and supports upgrades and life extension; Services legacy equipment from other manufacturers and offers multi-year agreements. Limit: Supplier support is not regulatory authority to grant life extension; customer or installed-base coverage is not exclusive share.

Has serial-supply capabilities for nuclear-island main equipment and turbine-generator sets for the conventional island. Limit: Group capabilities differ from listed-company financial scope; unqualified leadership/share language is not used; no publication date is shown.

H1 2026 revenue was EUR 2,696 million and EBITDA EUR 595 million; The company attributed Mining and Front End disruption to exceptional weather. Limit: Group results span multiple activities; do not extrapolate the half-year result; operational attribution is management's explanation.

EDF reports Framatome sales of EUR 5,372 million and Arabelle Solutions sales of EUR 990 million. Limit: Different from Framatome's own EUR 5,399 million disclosure; this source does not separately explain the EUR 27 million sales difference, so no specific cause is inferred; EDF electricity sales are not equipment-service revenue.

Manufactures reactor-pressure-vessel and steam-generator components and turbine/generator shafts; Highlights steelmaking, forging, heat treatment and large machining, and notes standardisation limits in build-to-order production. Limit: Used for manufacturing processes and business types rather than 2026 capacity; unqualified market-leadership claims are excluded.

The report lists Guohe-series reactor-coolant pumps and nuclear-island/conventional-island equipment supplied to Zhangzhou unit 1. Limit: Used as company evidence of equipment roles; total group revenue is not nuclear revenue, and no ranking without a comparable denominator is adopted.

KHNP signed the final two-unit Dukovany contract in June 2025; Its Barakah role includes joint project management and operating-support/long-term-maintenance agreements; Its El-Dabaa scope covers turbine-island construction for four VVER-1200 units. Limit: Contract scope differs by project; operator total revenue does not identify equipment/service revenue; no publication date is displayed.

Signed the Dukovany 5/6 A/E-services contract with KHNP on December 12, 2025; Scope includes auxiliary-equipment procurement and licensing support. Limit: This subcontracted engineering scope is neither total project investment nor fully recognised 2025 revenue.

Bechtel and Westinghouse selected Arabelle to supply three turbine-generator sets and related turbine-island equipment for Poland; Arabelle is an EDF Group subsidiary. Limit: Selection does not establish full financing, construction start or commercial operation; no contract value is stated; do not compare its ranking with nuclear-island suppliers.

Provides materials/component testing, safety and licensing support, outage inspections, lifecycle and waste management. Limit: The service catalogue is not revenue segmentation; parent-company relationship is evidenced by V07.

Safety-related parts require quality records, design compatibility and acceptance criteria; some OEMs reduce support or exit; Commercial-grade dedication, inspections and witnessed tests support qualification for nuclear use. Limit: Company guidance is not the governing regulation and does not imply unconditional acceptance of every commercial item in safety-related equipment.

Supports integrated plant assessment, time-limited aging analyses and environmental reporting; Licence extension requires regulatory approval. Limit: Supplier technical support does not replace regulatory approval; jurisdiction-specific rules require separate verification.

Long-term-operation services cover licence renewal, aging and asset management, modernisation and upgrades. Limit: The page describes capabilities rather than approval of a particular plant extension; publication date comes from structured page metadata.

WNA, Uranium Enrichment, updated 2026-09-29; 2025 global capacity; thousand SWU/year; capacity table and footnote. Supports enrichment-capacity composition; CNNC is estimated. Rows total 68,077 versus reported 68,076; author calculations use rows. The source does not explain the difference. Capacity is not revenue or deliveries.

WNA, World Nuclear Power Reactors & Uranium Requirements, updated 2026-10-08; global status snapshot; reactors/MWe; WORLD row and Notes. Supports fleet and construction indicators. Operable means grid-connected; construction includes suspended projects. Operable capacity is net and construction capacity gross; do not sum them.

Urenco, Full year 2025 audited financial results, published 2026-03-12; FY2025/2025-12-31 backlog; global group; EUR; Financial highlights/Outlook. Supports €2,096.2m revenue and €21.3bn backlog. Backlog spans multiple years; group scope and exchange-rate effects prevent treating it as annual segment-market size.

Urenco, Half year 2026 unaudited financial results, published 2026-08-13; H1 2026/2026-06-30; global group; EUR; Summary/backlog discussion. Supports €27.3bn backlog, €645.4m revenue and the delivery-timing explanation. Unaudited; do not mechanically annualize or infer falling demand from one revenue period.

Orano, Annual Activity Report 2025, issued 2026; exact PDF publication date not displayed; FY2025 and 2028–2030 expansion plans; French facility/global customers; million SWU/year; printed p.39. Supports 7.5 million existing capacity, 2.5 million expansion and its schedule. Expansion is prospective; the approximately 50-million-SWU demand market described in the report cannot replace the WNA capacity denominator.

Orano, 2026 Half-year Results, published 2026-07-31; H1/2026-06-30; global group; EUR; printed pp.2–3 and definitions. Supports €2,696m revenue, €34,393m backlog and €619m Front End revenue. Group figures include mining; Front End combines conversion and enrichment. Neither is a pure enrichment/equipment market total; backlog is a multi-year valuation.

EDF, Management Report 2025, released with results on 2026-02-20; FY2025; global Framatome/Arabelle; EUR; printed pp.10–11. EDF reports €5,372m Framatome sales versus €5,399m in M12. A complete revenue reconciliation is not provided in the reviewed texts. The narrative consistently uses M12.

EDF, 2026 half-year results, published 2026-07-31; H1 2026; global Framatome; EUR; printed p.6. Supports order intake of about €2.7bn and contributions from Installed Base/Fuel activities and EPR2 component production. Industry and services sales include other businesses and cannot be labelled Framatome sales; EBITDA, revenue and orders are distinct measures.

GE Vernova, 2025 Annual Report/10-K, issued 2026; FY2025; global; USD; 10-K printed pp.5 and 26. Supports Nuclear Power revenue of US$1,018m and BWR, fuel and SMR scope. Some nuclear-turbine activities sit in Steam Power, which also includes coal; total group/Power revenue is not nuclear revenue.

BWXT, FY2025 Form 10-K, signed 2026-02-23; FY2025; global group; USD; printed p.36, Commercial Operations. Supports US$853.070m revenue and US$231.0m acquisition contribution. Commercial Operations includes medical activities; group scope includes government/naval nuclear work. Growth is not entirely organic, and these figures cannot establish pure civil nuclear-power shares.

EDF, Universal Registration Document 2025, English PDF dated 2026-04-02; FY2025; global Framatome; product scope/reactors; printed pp.41–43. Supports nuclear steam-supply systems, instrumentation and control, fuel and operating-plant services, and work on more than 380 reactors. Service coverage overlaps and is not exclusive share; company scope also includes defence and healthcare.

Framatome, Framatome reports 2025 financial results, published 2026-03-04; FY2025; global group; EUR; financial table, commentary and EBITDA footnote. Supports €5,399m revenue, €5,924m orders and €665m EBITDA. The footnote explains adjustments versus EDF's €641m EBITDA; it does not separately reconcile the revenue difference. Adjacent businesses prevent treating group revenue as a pure nuclear-power market share.

Confirms operating dates and operator identity. Expected service life is forward-looking; achieved lifetime and returns are not established.
Same-day securities filing corroborates Unit 4 entering service. It does not establish costs, profit or future performance.
Supports Bechtel's 2017 appointment and project staffing. Project figures and supplier assessments cannot establish global industry outcomes.
Supports EBR-I's 1951 usable-electricity milestone. This definition differs from national-grid supply and full-scale commercial generation.
Undated announcement for a 2004 conference supports the June 1954 grid milestone. It does not establish a specific day.
Documents Calder Hall's generation, defuelling and subsequent stages. Completed fuel removal does not establish completed decommissioning.
Historical research supports commercialization and order cycles. The author does not represent IAEA; old forecasts are not current data.
DOE's retrospective supports accident mechanisms and training changes. The inaccessible NRC page and additional health conclusions are excluded.
INSAG-7 supports design, regulation and safety-culture findings. The accident investigation does not characterize every reactor design.
The 2015 technical volume supports external-event and defence findings. It provides neither present accident probabilities nor legal blame allocation.
The 2017 brochure supports treaty dates and obligation scope. Historical party counts are not presented as current.
Supports the 2022 estimate and weld-process issue. EUR 13.2 billion uses 2015 prices, excluding construction-period interest; final costs are unproven.
Supports first grid connection and further testing in December 2024. It does not establish full-power or sustained performance.
Supports ageing assessments and auditable documentation. Technical guidance does not substitute for plant-specific regulatory permission.
Supports Browns Ferry's 2025 permissions and reviews. Plant-specific permission cannot establish 80-year operation for all reactors.
The 2023 article supports SMR definition, examples and economic uncertainty. Historic design counts are not current totals.
Supports six 2024 deconversion frameworks. Contract ceilings and eligibility establish neither material delivery nor realised revenue.
Supports Sizewell C's decision, financing and target. Costs in 2024 prices and projected benefits are not realised results.
The 2019 report informs ageing-fleet history. Its capacity and average-age figures are not treated as current.
Supports financing and enrichment concentration in 2025. Capacity, revenue and future scenarios measure different things.
Supports the October 2026 workforce programme. Graduate numbers, resolved shortages and productivity gains are not demonstrated.
Supports April 2026 construction progress and EPC role. Commercial operation, competitive cost and regulatory firsts are not established.
The 2024 US explanation supports spent-fuel planning and community involvement. Global policy uniformity and completed disposal are unproven.
Supports Calder Hall's 1956 opening. The article's conflicting, unqualified first-grid claim is excluded.

Year-end conversion-service commitments totalled about 83 million kgU of UF6; Westinghouse participates as a subcontractor in the KHNP-led Dukovany project and has fuel-fabrication responsibilities for a specified period. Limit: Conversion kgU differs from enrichment SWU; the page does not state its publication date; Cameco's ownership-share figures are not Westinghouse's 100% revenue.

Westinghouse Operating Plants includes engineered equipment, reactor services and fuel products and services; Most recurring business is secured in advance under contracts lasting three to more than ten years; Cameco Fuel Services includes UO2, UF6 and heavy-water-reactor fuel bundles. Limit: Management's recurring-business description does not guarantee quarterly growth; customer coverage is not exclusive market share; illustrative economics in this section are not forecasts or guidance; publication date not independently verified.

2025 revenue was EUR 5,399 million, new orders EUR 5,924 million and EBITDA EUR 665 million; Growth involved EPR projects, fuel, I&C and installed-base services; Major-component work included North America and South Africa; replacement of four steam generators at Flamanville 2 began in November 2025. Limit: Use Framatome's own reporting perimeter; its footnote identifies EUR 641 million under EDF reporting, which must not be mixed with EUR 665 million; avoid the potentially stale ownership boilerplate.

2025 revenue was EUR 2,096.2 million and the year-end order book EUR 21.3 billion; Contracted orders extend into the 2040s. Limit: The order book spans multiple years rather than current revenue; exchange rates affect its euro value; it is not reactor-equipment revenue or global equipment market share.

2025 group revenue was EUR 5,138 million; A one-off Japanese-utility back-end contract contribution raised the 2024 comparison base; Revised end-of-lifecycle estimates affected 2025 adjusted earnings. Limit: The group includes mining and other activities; group revenue and its annual change do not measure the reactor-maintenance market.

Segments comprise Mining, Front End (Chemistry and Enrichment), and Back End (Recycling, Nuclear Packages and Services, Dismantling and Services, Engineering); Back End revenue was EUR 2,352 million in 2025. Limit: Back End includes recycling, packages and engineering and is not pure decommissioning revenue; publication date is not displayed.

Commercial Operations revenue was USD 853.070 million in 2025, with approximately USD 1,720 million in year-end backlog; The segment supplies heavy nuclear components, fuel, engineering and maintenance and also includes medical isotope and pharmaceutical-related activities; Kinectrics acquisition closed on May 20, 2025 and entered Commercial Operations; Commercial contracts include fixed-price and time-and-materials arrangements, with large custom-component and service revenue generally recognised over time. Limit: Commercial Operations is not pure civilian nuclear-power revenue; acquisitions affect growth; government and naval nuclear work is separate; backlog methodology need not match peers; date is the report signature date.

Commercial Operations revenue was USD 586.158 million in H1 2026; The segment's June 30 backlog was USD 1,600.454 million; Q2 growth included nuclear components, field services, fuel handling, medical activities and Kinectrics. Limit: Interim results are unaudited, include medical activities and acquisition effects, and should not be annualised by simple doubling.

2025 group sales were USD 3,498.372 million; Naval & Power sales were USD 1,503.002 million; Commercial nuclear solutions grew, while the segment also includes naval and process-industry activities. Limit: Neither figure is pure nuclear-power equipment-and-service revenue; total orders and backlog also include aerospace, defence and other business.

Supplies reactor-coolant-pump technology for AP1000; Provides nuclear products, parts, I&C, testing, field and obsolescence support, alongside defence nuclear business. Limit: Installed-product coverage and self-described leadership do not establish exclusive revenue market share; no publication date is shown.

A contract of about KRW 320 billion covers two steam-turbine and turbine-control-system sets for Dukovany 5 and 6; The counterparty is Czech subsidiary Doosan Skoda Power; ceremony held February 16, 2026; KHNP signed the principal project contract in June 2025. Limit: An intra-group contract cannot simply be added as sales of both companies; contract value is not current-year revenue or proof of commissioning.

Products include reactor and internals, steam generators, coolant pumps, pressurisers and fuel-handling equipment; MMIS covers control, monitoring, instrumentation and emergency safety functions. Limit: Do not use the company's unqualified 'largest supplier' claim as a ranking; equipment configurations differ by reactor type.

Supplies large castings and forgings for nuclear reactors and steam generators as well as turbine and generator components. Limit: The business also serves other generation technologies and industrial users; no pure nuclear revenue or share is established.

Provides component replacement, repair/refurbishment, routine and outage maintenance, upgrades, engineering and I&C replacement. Limit: A service menu identifies capabilities rather than revenue or a specific current contract for every offering.

The current name is GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy (GVH); Provides reactor technology, fuel and nuclear services; GE Vernova-led GNF operates fuel plants; Canadian activities support BWRX-300 deployment. Limit: GE Vernova group revenue must not be treated as nuclear-business revenue; the page has no publication date.

Activities span uranium production, enrichment, fabrication, domestic and international nuclear construction, generation and spent-fuel/radioactive-waste management. Limit: Self-reported rankings are not independent market-share evidence; generation and non-nuclear businesses broaden the group perimeter; total revenue is not an equipment-service market estimate; publication date is not stated.

Maintains turbines, generators and other turbine-island equipment and supports upgrades and life extension; Services legacy equipment from other manufacturers and offers multi-year agreements. Limit: Supplier support is not regulatory authority to grant life extension; customer or installed-base coverage is not exclusive share.

Has serial-supply capabilities for nuclear-island main equipment and turbine-generator sets for the conventional island. Limit: Group capabilities differ from listed-company financial scope; unqualified leadership/share language is not used; no publication date is shown.

H1 2026 revenue was EUR 2,696 million and EBITDA EUR 595 million; The company attributed Mining and Front End disruption to exceptional weather. Limit: Group results span multiple activities; do not extrapolate the half-year result; operational attribution is management's explanation.

EDF reports Framatome sales of EUR 5,372 million and Arabelle Solutions sales of EUR 990 million. Limit: Different from Framatome's own EUR 5,399 million disclosure; this source does not separately explain the EUR 27 million sales difference, so no specific cause is inferred; EDF electricity sales are not equipment-service revenue.

Manufactures reactor-pressure-vessel and steam-generator components and turbine/generator shafts; Highlights steelmaking, forging, heat treatment and large machining, and notes standardisation limits in build-to-order production. Limit: Used for manufacturing processes and business types rather than 2026 capacity; unqualified market-leadership claims are excluded.

The report lists Guohe-series reactor-coolant pumps and nuclear-island/conventional-island equipment supplied to Zhangzhou unit 1. Limit: Used as company evidence of equipment roles; total group revenue is not nuclear revenue, and no ranking without a comparable denominator is adopted.

KHNP signed the final two-unit Dukovany contract in June 2025; Its Barakah role includes joint project management and operating-support/long-term-maintenance agreements; Its El-Dabaa scope covers turbine-island construction for four VVER-1200 units. Limit: Contract scope differs by project; operator total revenue does not identify equipment/service revenue; no publication date is displayed.

Signed the Dukovany 5/6 A/E-services contract with KHNP on December 12, 2025; Scope includes auxiliary-equipment procurement and licensing support. Limit: This subcontracted engineering scope is neither total project investment nor fully recognised 2025 revenue.

Bechtel and Westinghouse selected Arabelle to supply three turbine-generator sets and related turbine-island equipment for Poland; Arabelle is an EDF Group subsidiary. Limit: Selection does not establish full financing, construction start or commercial operation; no contract value is stated; do not compare its ranking with nuclear-island suppliers.

Provides materials/component testing, safety and licensing support, outage inspections, lifecycle and waste management. Limit: The service catalogue is not revenue segmentation; parent-company relationship is evidenced by V07.

Safety-related parts require quality records, design compatibility and acceptance criteria; some OEMs reduce support or exit; Commercial-grade dedication, inspections and witnessed tests support qualification for nuclear use. Limit: Company guidance is not the governing regulation and does not imply unconditional acceptance of every commercial item in safety-related equipment.

Supports integrated plant assessment, time-limited aging analyses and environmental reporting; Licence extension requires regulatory approval. Limit: Supplier technical support does not replace regulatory approval; jurisdiction-specific rules require separate verification.

Long-term-operation services cover licence renewal, aging and asset management, modernisation and upgrades. Limit: The page describes capabilities rather than approval of a particular plant extension; publication date comes from structured page metadata.

WNA, Uranium Enrichment, updated 2026-09-29; 2025 global capacity; thousand SWU/year; capacity table and footnote. Supports enrichment-capacity composition; CNNC is estimated. Rows total 68,077 versus reported 68,076; author calculations use rows. The source does not explain the difference. Capacity is not revenue or deliveries.

WNA, World Nuclear Power Reactors & Uranium Requirements, updated 2026-10-08; global status snapshot; reactors/MWe; WORLD row and Notes. Supports fleet and construction indicators. Operable means grid-connected; construction includes suspended projects. Operable capacity is net and construction capacity gross; do not sum them.

Urenco, Full year 2025 audited financial results, published 2026-03-12; FY2025/2025-12-31 backlog; global group; EUR; Financial highlights/Outlook. Supports €2,096.2m revenue and €21.3bn backlog. Backlog spans multiple years; group scope and exchange-rate effects prevent treating it as annual segment-market size.

Urenco, Half year 2026 unaudited financial results, published 2026-08-13; H1 2026/2026-06-30; global group; EUR; Summary/backlog discussion. Supports €27.3bn backlog, €645.4m revenue and the delivery-timing explanation. Unaudited; do not mechanically annualize or infer falling demand from one revenue period.

Orano, Annual Activity Report 2025, issued 2026; exact PDF publication date not displayed; FY2025 and 2028–2030 expansion plans; French facility/global customers; million SWU/year; printed p.39. Supports 7.5 million existing capacity, 2.5 million expansion and its schedule. Expansion is prospective; the approximately 50-million-SWU demand market described in the report cannot replace the WNA capacity denominator.

Orano, 2026 Half-year Results, published 2026-07-31; H1/2026-06-30; global group; EUR; printed pp.2–3 and definitions. Supports €2,696m revenue, €34,393m backlog and €619m Front End revenue. Group figures include mining; Front End combines conversion and enrichment. Neither is a pure enrichment/equipment market total; backlog is a multi-year valuation.

EDF, Management Report 2025, released with results on 2026-02-20; FY2025; global Framatome/Arabelle; EUR; printed pp.10–11. EDF reports €5,372m Framatome sales versus €5,399m in M12. A complete revenue reconciliation is not provided in the reviewed texts. The narrative consistently uses M12.

EDF, 2026 half-year results, published 2026-07-31; H1 2026; global Framatome; EUR; printed p.6. Supports order intake of about €2.7bn and contributions from Installed Base/Fuel activities and EPR2 component production. Industry and services sales include other businesses and cannot be labelled Framatome sales; EBITDA, revenue and orders are distinct measures.

GE Vernova, 2025 Annual Report/10-K, issued 2026; FY2025; global; USD; 10-K printed pp.5 and 26. Supports Nuclear Power revenue of US$1,018m and BWR, fuel and SMR scope. Some nuclear-turbine activities sit in Steam Power, which also includes coal; total group/Power revenue is not nuclear revenue.

BWXT, FY2025 Form 10-K, signed 2026-02-23; FY2025; global group; USD; printed p.36, Commercial Operations. Supports US$853.070m revenue and US$231.0m acquisition contribution. Commercial Operations includes medical activities; group scope includes government/naval nuclear work. Growth is not entirely organic, and these figures cannot establish pure civil nuclear-power shares.

EDF, Universal Registration Document 2025, English PDF dated 2026-04-02; FY2025; global Framatome; product scope/reactors; printed pp.41–43. Supports nuclear steam-supply systems, instrumentation and control, fuel and operating-plant services, and work on more than 380 reactors. Service coverage overlaps and is not exclusive share; company scope also includes defence and healthcare.

Framatome, Framatome reports 2025 financial results, published 2026-03-04; FY2025; global group; EUR; financial table, commentary and EBITDA footnote. Supports €5,399m revenue, €5,924m orders and €665m EBITDA. The footnote explains adjustments versus EDF's €641m EBITDA; it does not separately reconcile the revenue difference. Adjacent businesses prevent treating group revenue as a pure nuclear-power market share.

IAEA Imagebank photograph 03210491 by Petr Pavlicek / IAEA, taken 2012-11-06 and uploaded 2013-03-18. The original-size page and downloaded JPEG both show 3000 × 2000 pixels. The source page links CC BY-SA 2.0, permitting redistribution with attribution and its licence. The original file is included unchanged and displayed proportionally. It depicts the existing Dukovany plant and cannot prove later new-build progress or supplier relationships. Licence https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/ . Provides component replacement, repair/refurbishment, routine and outage maintenance, upgrades, engineering and I&C replacement. Limit: A service menu identifies capabilities rather than revenue or a specific current contract for every offering.

H1 2026 revenue was EUR 2,696 million and EBITDA EUR 595 million; The company attributed Mining and Front End disruption to exceptional weather. Limit: Group results span multiple activities; do not extrapolate the half-year result; operational attribution is management's explanation.

Manufactures reactor-pressure-vessel and steam-generator components and turbine/generator shafts; Highlights steelmaking, forging, heat treatment and large machining, and notes standardisation limits in build-to-order production. Limit: Used for manufacturing processes and business types rather than 2026 capacity; unqualified market-leadership claims are excluded.

Unitree G1 humanoid robot and Go2 quadruped on an exhibition stage at Japan Mobility Show 2025, Tokyo Big Sight, October 31, 2025. The photograph illustrates robot hardware and does not establish industrial autonomy. Photo: RuinDig / Yuki Uchida, via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY 4.0. Original photograph; reproduced without pixel changes.
For web display, the photograph has been proportionally resized and compressed; the downloadable original is unchanged.

Sources current to 12 October 2026. This report covers the global embodied intelligence ecosystem, with humanoid commercialization as a focus. Our central assessment is that defined tasks now have early commercial evidence, while dependable generalization, operating cost and application safety still determine the path to scale. Three separate charts retain their own market definitions, periods and metrics. None establishes company shares across the whole embodied intelligence industry.

notes: Downstream is where these technologies acquire an economic purpose. Manufacturers need reliable loading, handling, sorting and inspection. Logistics operators need dependable transfer between equipment already in place. Research and education customers need development access and repeatable experiments. Household buyers need useful assistance in variable spaces. These are distinct customer jobs, rather than a single interchangeable market. An integrator, fleet operator or service team connects the robot to the actual work: defining the task, arranging interfaces, accepting the installation, managing exceptions and supporting operation. The value created must be demonstrated for each application.

Three business-model categories help organize the evidence. Equipment sales transfer a machine and associated obligations under a specified package. The GXO–Agility agreement illustrates Robots-as-a-Service; AGIBOT offers data services. These categories do not imply identical risk allocation: buyers still need to examine who pays for integration, downtime, remote assistance and replacement parts. An appealing subscription price can coexist with substantial implementation work, just as a low hardware price can coexist with an expensive development project. [H02] [V13]

The report's analytical conclusion is that competition occurs at several levels simultaneously. Component firms compete on controllable performance and supply quality; infrastructure firms on development and deployment capability; robot makers on a usable machine; and application providers on an accepted outcome. A manufacturer's role, a robot's body shape and its operating maturity should therefore be shown separately. For downstream purchasing, the most informative comparison is the cost and quality of a completed job under the same conditions. A catalog specification, a cumulative production count and a successful demonstration each provide useful evidence, but answer different questions.

Industry → upstream midstream downstream → segments → representative companies or products. The map is an analytical classification, not a list of verified supply contracts. Several firms appear in multiple roles; early product programs remain identified as such in the text.

articles.title: Global Solid Waste Management and Resource Recovery Industry Brief

citations.text: Photo: STEINERT, “STEINERT UniSort PR” · CC BY 4.0 · 29 January 2019. Original photograph unchanged; responsive web versions resized and the display may be cropped to fit. Image evidence I01 .
notes: Industry report · Version 1.1 · Global market · Public information cutoff 10 October 2026.

This report examines municipal solid waste, commercial and industrial residues, construction and demolition materials, hazardous waste, and electronic waste through the businesses that collect, treat and recover them. Agricultural residues and mining wastes are discussed where relevant to material recovery; wastewater services and primary mining are outside the core scope. Statistical boundaries vary, so the report does not present an invented aggregate for every solid-waste stream.

The central finding is that reliable collection, permitted treatment and saleable recovered outputs determine commercial value together. Service revenue can remain resilient while recycled commodity prices weaken. A large physical waste burden does not automatically become a profitable addressable market: someone must fund collection, pay for safe disposal, and purchase recovered materials.

All monetary figures retain their original currencies and accounting definitions. The company comparison uses 2025 full-year disclosures; Sims has a June financial year-end. Later public policy and statistical publications are included through the cutoff. Forecasts are identified as forecasts. The treatment-pathway chart covers municipal solid waste only; the company comparison retains each business's distinct reporting scope.

citations.section: The global municipal waste processing mix
citations.text: Source: Cook, Ionkova, Bhada-Tata, Yadav and van Woerden (2026), What a Waste 3.0, World Bank, Figure 2.16, printed page 29, PDF page 65 [15]
notes: Shares of global municipal solid waste generated by mass; World Bank's modeled 2022 baseline. National observations are harmonized and weighted by 2022 waste generation. Published integer percentages sum to 100%. This chart is not company market share or a breakdown of all solid-waste streams.
Use the seven original published percentages directly. 17+15+6+20+17+12+13=100. No normalization, midpoint substitution, or reverse calculation of absolute tonnes.

2022 baseline modeled/weighted aggregate. National treatment observations can come from differing years, predominantly 2020-24. Shares are weighted by 2022 waste generation. Original country and city data are adjusted for missing flows including uncollected waste, informal-sector collection and nonhousehold MSW. See section 1.2, printed pages 5-7, and Appendix C.
Use the report's seven categories as published. Uncollected waste remains a distinct category; do not add self-managed uncollected burning, dumping, recycling or composting as additional slices.
No separate unknown slice is published in Figure 2.16. This does not imply every physical flow was measured: World Bank notes conservative model adjustments may still leave unrecorded flows.

Original Figure 2.16 says Incineration. Section 1.2 printed p. 5 / PDF p. 41 expressly defines all incineration references in the report as incineration with energy recovery. Recycling is separately classified from composting and anaerobic digestion; no unsupported reuse expansion.

The seven published shares are uncollected 17%, recycling 15%, composting and anaerobic digestion 6%, incineration with energy recovery 20%, sanitary landfill 17%, controlled landfill 12%, and dumpsites 13%. Their sum is 100%, using the source's integer percentages without normalization or inferred decimal precision. The World Bank defines references to incineration in this report as incineration with energy recovery. [15]

This is a harmonized, mass-weighted 2022 baseline, built from country observations that predominantly cover 2020–2024 and adjusted for missing flows. It is not a simultaneous 2022 census of every plant. Uncollected waste is a separate category; adding self-managed burning or dumping as new slices would count some flows twice. Neither the recycling slice nor the composting-and-digestion slice should be interpreted as a yield of saleable material. [15]

The commercial implication is an analytical judgment: spending opportunities differ between an unserved collection area and a mature market upgrading material quality. The chart shows the physical system's structure, without allocating revenue to companies or including every industrial waste stream.

Global perspective with comparison of China the United States and Europe

The industry's central task is to convert spending and orders into functioning network capacity. This report explains the technologies, supplier roles and regional demand behind that task, then examines the constraints on delivery.

The core scope is electricity transmission and distribution equipment. Project services and network investment are discussed as adjacent activities and demand context. Company examples are illustrative. The mandatory share figure uses the user-approved China panel-radiator component market in 2025; it is explicitly not a global or whole-industry share. Bracketed IDs connect claims and figures to the separate Supporting Evidence appendix.

citations.text: Read the original source
notes: Title: DOE and Industry Team Up to Keep the Lights On for America. Publisher: U.S. Department of Energy. Material: primary government workshop account.
Published on 22 February 2024. Event: March 2023 workshop and 2023 supply conditions. Statistical comparison: 2019–2023. Read: 8 October 2026.
Coverage: U.S. distribution transformers. Locator: supply-stress and workshop passages. Relevant unit: months.
Supports: Supports lead times rising from 3–6 months in 2019 to 12–30 months in 2023, constraints in GOES, aluminium, copper and skilled workforce, and design-standardization efforts.

Limitations: This is a dated government account of the U.S. distribution segment. It cannot substitute for large-transformer or worldwide 2026 delivery data. Proposed supply responses are not evidence that shortages have ended or a new factory already delivers full rated output.

notes: Panel radiators used on transformers rated 110 kV and above. This is a narrow component market, not all transformers or all grid equipment.
China domestic market · Estimated market share by sales volume (%)

The Transformer Branch of the China Electrical Equipment Industry Association surveyed sales volumes of major domestic radiator-producing member firms, then extrapolated nationally. The issuer/sponsor filing reproduces the association estimate; it is primary evidence of the disclosure, not a census of the whole market. Other manufacturers = 100.00 - 14.72 = 85.28; total = 100.00%. Two decimal places as disclosed; no additional precision inferred. Raw survey data, sample coverage, numerical numerator/denominator and extrapolation formula were not disclosed. The physical sales-volume unit was not specified. Financial consolidation entities and elimination of related-party/internal sales were not specified for the share numerator. Other manufacturers is a calculated residual, not separately observed data; no individual competitor share or total market volume was disclosed. Source [M09], printed p58.

citations.section: [M09] Response to the IPO application review inquiry for Youbang Radiator (Changshu) Co., Ltd.
citations.text: Read the original source
notes: Issuer/sponsor BSE reply, prepared June 2026, disclosed 2 July 2026; read 8 October 2026. Printed p 58 (PDF index 58); repeated p 19, verification procedure p 63.

Scope: China's domestic plate radiators for transformers rated 110 kV and above; calendar 2025; sales-volume share (%). Lower voltages and other transformer cooling systems fall outside this definition. This is not grid-industry share.
The Transformer Branch of the China Electrical Equipment Industry Association reported Youbang at 14.72% (2024: 13.31%), surveying major domestic member suppliers then extrapolating nationally.

The filing verifies disclosure; measurement remains an association estimate, not a census. Raw data, coverage, volume unit, numerator/denominator and extrapolation formula are absent; consolidation and related-party eliminations are unspecified. Banking-review entities do not define share scope.
Other manufacturers=100−14.72=85.28%; total 100%. This residual inherits uncertainty. No competitor shares or market volume are disclosed. Link originals; reproduction rights unverified.

notes: Panel radiators used on transformers rated 110 kV and above. This is a narrow component market, not all transformers or all grid equipment.
China domestic market · Estimated market share by sales volume (%)

citations.section: The value chain and who gets paid
citations.text: Download PNG · Download editable SVG · Download source data (CSV)
notes: Upstream, institutions provide accounts, liquidity and the technical standards that let a payment credential work across different devices and providers. EMVCo maintains specifications; it is not itself a merchant acquirer or a settlement network. EMV payment tokenisation substitutes a constrained token for the primary account number, allowing existing card infrastructure to support digital use cases. A payment token in this sense is distinct from a blockchain asset. [H06] [R02]

Midstream, the card scheme sets participation and transaction rules while its processing network helps institutions exchange messages. Acquirers and processors connect merchants, perform operational work and arrange payment acceptance. Adyen is an example of a company providing both processing and acquiring. Its documentation makes an instructive distinction: funds received by Adyen in a settled payment have not necessarily been paid out to the merchant. Provider receipt and merchant payout are different events. [R01]

Downstream, wallets, checkout software and terminals make these services usable in commerce. A card held in Apple Pay or Google Pay may still rely on the underlying card network; the wallet is not automatically an independent clearing rail. UPI and Pix illustrate a different category: account-payment arrangements whose adoption depends on participant access, governance and useful payment scenarios. The diagram classifies roles, not market shares or verified supply contracts. [H07] [H14]
Figure 1 Retail payment infrastructure value chain

Figure 1 follows the same sequence as the text: foundations, networks and acceptance, then access and commerce. A company can occupy several positions, and an institution providing a payment interface may rely on another institution for settlement. Names are representative rather than exhaustive. Sources: [H06] [H07] [H13] [H14] [M01] [R01] [R02] .

In a four-party card arrangement, the consumer deals with an issuer and the merchant with an acquirer, while the network coordinates their interaction. Interchange generally flows from the acquirer to the issuer. Scheme and processing fees are separate, and the merchant service charge contains several components. Treating the entire merchant charge as Visa or Mastercard revenue misidentifies both the recipient and the economics. [H07]

Our interpretation is that a new network faces a coordination problem before it faces a computing problem. Issuers need merchants willing to accept the credential; merchants need enough potential buyers; both need reliable operation and agreed procedures when a transaction goes wrong. Discounting one side can attract participants, but the discount has to be funded. Scale is valuable only if the network can retain useful participation after incentives and operating costs.

Regional analysis changes the competitive question. A globally aggregated card chart combines markets with different institutions and payment habits. In the United States, routing and network contracting feature in the DOJ debit case. In Europe, interchange regulation and instant-transfer rules constrain different layers of the service. India and Brazil illustrate how account-payment systems can develop around domestic institutions. These observations should be compared as institutional settings, not combined into a fabricated worldwide payment-method share. [H09] [H12] [H14] [H15]
